books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Democratic conventions of 1860 as told in Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 7, Topic 5.7, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 14. Dates and the walkout verified against the 1860 Democratic National Conventions record (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_Democratic_National_Conventions) and the OSU eHistory chronology. The facts are as stated in the books; the wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: In April 1860 the Democrats met at Charleston, South Carolina, to choose a presidential candidate. Stephen A. Douglas led the voting, but Southern delegates demanded a platform promising that the federal government would protect slavery in the territories. When the convention refused, delegates from eight Southern states walked out, and the convention broke up without naming a nominee. The party met again in Baltimore in June and split in two: Northern Democrats nominated Douglas, and Southern Democrats nominated Vice President John C. Breckinridge.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The events described in the passage most directly led to which result in the election of 1860?

options.text: The Republican Party adopted Douglas's platform.
options.misconception: Background: the Republicans ran Lincoln on a platform of their own, opposing the spread of slavery, not on Douglas's platform.

options.text: The Constitutional Union Party won the Deep South.
options.misconception: Background: Breckinridge's Southern Democrats carried the Deep South; Bell's Constitutional Union Party won the Upper South.

options.text: The Democratic vote was divided between two candidates.
Lincoln lost every Northern state to Douglas.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln swept nearly all the Northern states; Douglas carried only Missouri and part of New Jersey.

rationales.A: Background: the Republicans ran Lincoln on a platform of their own, opposing the spread of slavery, not on Douglas's platform.
rationales.B: Background: Breckinridge's Southern Democrats carried the Deep South; Bell's Constitutional Union Party won the Upper South.
rationales.C: The passage ends with the party split in two, each half nominating its own man. Background: two Democratic nominees on the ballot split the party's vote, and Lincoln won the Electoral College against the divided field.
rationales.D: Background: Lincoln swept nearly all the Northern states; Douglas carried only Missouri and part of New Jersey.
rationales.general:
1. Follow the passage: one party walks in, two parties walk out.
2. Two Democratic nominees meant two Democratic vote totals in November.
3. Background: Lincoln needed only a plurality in each Northern state, and the split gave it to him.
4. A divided party cannot win a winner-take-all race.
Remember: when a party splits, count the votes it loses to itself before counting the opponent's.
